source_paragraphs: You must dispose of any waste fuel oil or mix of oil and water that collects in the bund without causing pollution.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The Environment Agency can serve a notice to stop a farmer using an unsuitable silage, slurry or agricultural fuel oil store until it is improved or relocated, if there is a significant risk of pollution.
source_paragraphs: The Environment Agency can serve a notice to stop you using an unsuitable silage, slurry or agricultural fuel oil store until it's improved or relocated. They'll do this if they think there's a significant risk of pollution – for example if you've not allowed enough capacity to store slurry.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer served a notice must be given at least 28 days to carry out the required work.
source_paragraphs: You'll have at least 28 days to carry out the work. You may be allowed more time, for example if you need planning permission or the weather is unsuitable.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer wishing to appeal against a notice must do so within 28 days from the day after the notice was served.
source_paragraphs: If you disagree with the notice, you can appeal. You have 28 days from the day after the notice was served.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: An appeal against a notice must be made in writing to the Secretary of State for the Environment and Rural Affairs.
source_paragraphs: Appeal in writing to the Secretary of State.
Your letter must explain why you're appealing.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The rules for silage, slurry and agricultural fuel oil storage are based on the Water Resources (Control of Pollution) (Silage, Slurry and Agricultural Fuel Oil) (England) Regulations (SSAFO regulations).
source_paragraphs: These rules are based on the Water Resources (Control of Pollution) (Silage, Slurry and Agricultural Fuel Oil) (England) Regulations – known as the SSAFO regulations – and related legislation.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A livestock manure holder in a nitrate vulnerable zone may apply up to 170kg per hectare of nitrogen in livestock manure on their holding in each calendar year.
source_paragraphs: You can apply up to 170kg per hectare of nitrogen in livestock manure on your holding in a nitrate vulnerable zone ( NVZ ) in each calendar year.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The 170kg per hectare nitrogen loading limit applies as an average across the whole holding, including manure deposited directly by grazing livestock and what is spread.
source_paragraphs: This includes manure deposited directly by grazing livestock and what you spread. This limit is the loading limit and applies as an average across your holding.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer may operate under a derogation to use up to 250kg of nitrogen per hectare from grazing livestock manure under certain conditions.
source_paragraphs: You may be able to operate under a derogation to use up to 250kg of nitrogen per hectare from grazing livestock manure under certain conditions.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer may apply for a grassland derogation to use up to 250kg of nitrogen per hectare if the nitrogen comes from grazing livestock manure.
source_paragraphs: You can apply for a grassland derogation to use a higher limit of up to 250kg of nitrogen per hectare, if the nitrogen comes from grazing livestock manure.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Grazing livestock for the purposes of the grassland derogation are: cattle (except veal calves), sheep, deer, goats, and horses.
source_paragraphs:
Grazing livestock are:
cattle (except for veal calves)
sheep
deer
goats
horses

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer cannot obtain permission to use more than 170kg of nitrogen per hectare from non-grazing livestock (veal calves, pigs, or poultry) and must keep within the 170kg per hectare limit for such livestock.
source_paragraphs: You cannot get permission to use more nitrogen from non-grazing livestock (veal calves, pigs or poultry) and must keep within the 170kg per hectare limit.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer whose derogation application is successful must comply with the conditions of the derogation and the NVZ rules.
source_paragraphs: You must comply with the conditions of a derogation and the NVZ rules if your application is successful.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer may only apply for a grassland derogation if at least 80% of the agricultural area of their holding is grass.
source_paragraphs: You can only apply for a derogation if at least 80% of the agricultural area of your holding is grass.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The agricultural area is the part of a holding used for agricultural purposes and does not include surface waters, areas of hardstanding, buildings or woodland (unless woodland is used for grazing), or any land covered by a greenhouse.
source_paragraphs:
The agricultural area is the part of your holding you use for agricultural purposes. It does not include, for example:
surface waters
areas of hardstanding
buildings or woodland (unless the woodland is used for grazing)
any land covered by a greenhouse

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer must apply between 10 November and 31 December 2025 for a grassland derogation in 2026.
source_paragraphs: You must apply between 10 November and 31 December 2025 for a grassland derogation in 2026.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When applying for a derogation, a farmer must provide their farm name, address, County Parish Holding (CPH) number, and a map showing the location and extent of the land parcels that make up their holding.
source_paragraphs:
When you apply, you must give the:
farm name, address and your County Parish Holding (CPH) number and provide a map showing the location and extent of the land parcels that make up your holding

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When applying for a derogation, a farmer must provide the agricultural area and grassland area of their farm in hectares on 1 January of the year for which they are applying.
source_paragraphs: agricultural area and grassland area of your farm in hectares on 1 January of the year for which you are applying

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When applying for a derogation, a farmer must provide the amount of manure nitrogen produced by grazing livestock kept on their farm during the calendar year in kilograms of nitrogen (kgN).
source_paragraphs: amount of manure nitrogen produced by grazing livestock kept on your farm during the calendar year in kilograms of nitrogen ( kgN )

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When applying for a derogation, a farmer must provide the amount of manure nitrogen produced by grazing livestock they intend to bring onto or send off their farm during the calendar year (kgN).
source_paragraphs: amount of manure nitrogen produced by grazing livestock you intend to bring onto or send off your farm during the calendar year ( kgN )

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When applying for a derogation, a farmer must provide the total amount of manure nitrogen from grazing livestock on their farm during the calendar year (kgN).
source_paragraphs: total amount of manure nitrogen from grazing livestock on your farm during the calendar year ( kgN )

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When applying for a derogation, a farmer must provide the amount of manure nitrogen produced by non-grazing livestock on their farm during the calendar year (kgN).
source_paragraphs: amount of manure nitrogen produced by non-grazing livestock on your farm during the calendar year ( kgN )

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When applying for a derogation, a farmer must provide the amount of manure nitrogen produced by non-grazing livestock they intend to bring onto or send off their farm during the calendar year (kgN).
source_paragraphs: amount of manure nitrogen produced by non-grazing livestock you intend to bring onto or send off your farm during the calendar year ( kgN )

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When applying for a derogation, a farmer must provide the total amount of manure nitrogen from non-grazing livestock on their farm during the calendar year (kgN).
source_paragraphs: total amount of manure nitrogen from non-grazing livestock on your farm during the calendar year ( kgN )

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a derogation application is successful, the farmer must formally agree in writing to the Environment Agency to fulfil the conditions of their derogation.
source_paragraphs: If your application is successful, you must formally agree to fulfil the conditions of your derogation in writing to the EA .

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The Environment Agency will refuse a derogation application if the farmer does not meet the eligibility criteria or does not apply within the specified dates.
source_paragraphs: The EA will refuse your application if you do not meet the eligibility criteria or do not apply within the specified dates. If refused, the EA expects you to follow the 170kg nitrogen per hectare limit.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a derogation application is refused, the Environment Agency expects the farmer to follow the 170kg nitrogen per hectare limit.
source_paragraphs: If refused, the EA expects you to follow the 170kg nitrogen per hectare limit.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The Environment Agency is required to carry out a Habitats Regulations Assessment (HRA) if a farm falls within or is near a European site designated under the Habitats Regulations, or is within the catchment of a European site in unfavourable conservation status due to nutrient pollution.
source_paragraphs: The EA are required to carry out a Habitats Regulations Assessment (HRA) if your farm falls within or is near a European site designated under the Habitats Regulations or your farm is within the catchment of a European site that is in unfavourable conservation status due to nutrient pollution.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a Habitats Regulations Assessment shows that granting a derogation would have an adverse effect on a European site, the derogation application may be refused.
source_paragraphs: If the HRA shows that granting a derogation would have an adverse effect on a European site your application may be refused.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The Environment Agency may refuse to give a derogation if the farmer had a derogation during a previous year but did not follow all the conditions for that derogation.
source_paragraphs: The EA may also refuse to give you a derogation if you had a derogation during a previous year but did not follow all the conditions for that derogation.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer may appeal a refused derogation application within 30 days of the refusal, and an independent panel will consider the appeal.
source_paragraphs: You can appeal within 30 days of your application being refused. An independent panel will consider your appeal.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must meet all the conditions of their derogation and follow the rules that apply when using nitrogen fertilisers and storing organic manures in NVZs.
source_paragraphs: You must meet all the conditions of your derogation and follow the rules that apply when using nitrogen fertilisers and storing organic manures in NVZs .

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a farmer does not meet the conditions of a derogation for the year it covers, the Environment Agency may fine them.
source_paragraphs:
If you do not meet the conditions of a derogation for the year it covers:
the EA may fine you

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a farmer does not meet the conditions of a derogation for the year it covers, they may not be eligible to apply for a derogation in the following year.
source_paragraphs:
If you do not meet the conditions of a derogation for the year it covers:
you may not be eligible to apply for a derogation in the following year

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer will not be allowed to apply more than 170kg of nitrogen per hectare in livestock manure, averaged across their holding, if the Environment Agency withdraws their derogation.
source_paragraphs:
You will not be allowed to apply more than 170kg of nitrogen per hectare in livestock manure, averaged across your holding, if the EA either:
withdraws your derogation
decides you're ineligible to apply for a derogation the following year

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A farmer will not be allowed to apply more than 170kg of nitrogen per hectare in livestock manure, averaged across their holding, if the Environment Agency decides they are ineligible to apply for a derogation the following year.
source_paragraphs:
You will not be allowed to apply more than 170kg of nitrogen per hectare in livestock manure, averaged across your holding, if the EA either:
withdraws your derogation
decides you're ineligible to apply for a derogation the following year

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a derogation holder ploughs grassland, they must plant a crop with a high nitrogen demand (for example, grass, potatoes, sugar beet, maize) within 4 weeks from the date of ploughing.
source_paragraphs:
If you plough grassland where you have a derogation, you must plant one of the following:
a crop with a high nitrogen demand (for example, grass, potatoes, sugar beet, maize) within 4 weeks from the date of ploughing
grass within 6 weeks from the date of ploughing

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a derogation holder ploughs grassland, they must plant grass within 6 weeks from the date of ploughing.
source_paragraphs:
If you plough grassland where you have a derogation, you must plant one of the following:
a crop with a high nitrogen demand (for example, grass, potatoes, sugar beet, maize) within 4 weeks from the date of ploughing
grass within 6 weeks from the date of ploughing

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must not plough temporary grassland on sandy soils between 1 July and 31 December.
source_paragraphs: You must not plough temporary grassland on sandy soils between 1 July and 31 December.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must not plough any area of grass before 16 January if they spread livestock manure on that area in the previous year between 1 September and 31 December on sandy soils.
source_paragraphs:
You must not plough any area of grass before 16 January if you've spread livestock manure on that area in the previous year between:
1 September and 31 December on sandy soils
15 October and 15 January on all other soils

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must not plough any area of grass before 16 January if they spread livestock manure on that area in the previous year between 15 October and 15 January on all other soils.
source_paragraphs:
You must not plough any area of grass before 16 January if you've spread livestock manure on that area in the previous year between:
1 September and 31 December on sandy soils
15 October and 15 January on all other soils

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must not grow leguminous or other atmospheric nitrogen-fixing plants in their rotation, except grass with less than 50% clover or legumes under-sown with grass.
source_paragraphs:
You must not grow leguminous or other atmospheric nitrogen-fixing plants in your rotation, except:
grass with less than 50% clover
legumes under-sown with grass

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must plan the amount of phosphate fertiliser they put on their land in an NVZ.
source_paragraphs: You must plan the amount of phosphate fertiliser you put on your land in an NVZ .

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before using phosphate for the first time in a field where a crop is to be planted or has been planted, a derogation holder must calculate the amount of phosphate in the soil likely to be available for the crop during the growing season.
source_paragraphs:
You must take the following steps before you use phosphate for the first time in a field where you're going to plant a crop or have planted a crop:
Calculate the amount of phosphate in the soil that's likely to be available for the crop to use during the growing season.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before using phosphate for the first time in a field, a derogation holder must calculate the amount of phosphate that should be applied to the crop to get the best crops, taking into account the phosphate already available in the soil.
source_paragraphs: Calculate the amount of phosphate that should be applied to the crop to get the best crops, taking into account the phosphate already available in the soil.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before using phosphate for the first time in a field, a derogation holder must calculate the amount of phosphate from any planned applications of organic manure that is likely to be available to the crop in the growing season in which it is spread.
source_paragraphs: Calculate the amount of phosphate from any planned applications of organic manure that's likely to be available to the crop in the growing season in which you spread it.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before using phosphate for the first time in a field, a derogation holder must calculate the amount of manufactured phosphate fertiliser they will need.
source_paragraphs: Calculate the amount of manufactured phosphate fertiliser you will need.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must carry out phosphate availability from organic manure and manufactured phosphate calculations every time they spread manure or fertiliser.
source_paragraphs: You must also carry out steps 3 and 4 every time you spread manure or fertiliser.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before using manure or fertiliser on any crop (including grass) in following growing seasons, a derogation holder must repeat the calculations for phosphate in the soil and the amount that should be applied.
source_paragraphs:
Before you use manure or fertiliser on any crop (including grass) in following growing seasons, you must:
repeat steps 1 and 2
plan your fertiliser use for that growing season

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before using manure or fertiliser on any crop (including grass) in following growing seasons, a derogation holder must plan their fertiliser use for that growing season.
source_paragraphs:
Before you use manure or fertiliser on any crop (including grass) in following growing seasons, you must:
repeat steps 1 and 2
plan your fertiliser use for that growing season

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: For permanent grassland, phosphate calculations must be made based on the farming year starting on 1 January.
source_paragraphs: For permanent grassland, make your calculations based on the farming year starting on 1 January.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must sample and analyse the soil at least once every 4 years to determine the amount of phosphorus available to crops during the growing season.
source_paragraphs: You must sample and analyse the soil at least once every 4 years. This will tell you the amount of phosphorus in the soil that's likely to be available for the crop to use during the growing season.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must carry out soil sampling and analysis for at least every 5 hectares of their holding that has the same cropping and soil type.
source_paragraphs: You must do this for at least every 5 hectares of your holding that has the same cropping and soil type.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder may use existing soil sampling results if they are less than 4 years old when the derogation starts.
source_paragraphs: You can use existing soil sampling results if they're less than 4 years old when your derogation starts.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a derogation holder does not have soil sampling data that is less than 4 years old, they must sample 75% of their farm area in the first year of the derogation.
source_paragraphs: If you have not got sampling data that's less than 4 years old, you'll need to sample 75% of your farm area in the first year of your derogation. You then need to sample the remaining 25% of your farm area in the year of your next derogation.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must sample the remaining 25% of their farm area in the year of their next derogation if they sampled 75% in the first year.
source_paragraphs: You then need to sample the remaining 25% of your farm area in the year of your next derogation.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must record their nitrogen use and any phosphate they use from manufactured fertilisers and organic manures in their fertilisation plan and field records.
source_paragraphs:
In your fertilisation plan and field records you must record your nitrogen use and any phosphate you use from:
manufactured fertilisers
organic manures

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must record how much phosphate and nitrogen any manure contains within one week of bringing it onto their holding.
source_paragraphs: You must record how much phosphate and nitrogen any manure contains within one week of bringing it onto your holding.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a derogation holder does not know the phosphate content of manure brought onto their farm, they must analyse or calculate the amount and record it within a week of finding it out.
source_paragraphs: If you do not know the phosphate content of manure you bring onto your farm, you must analyse or calculate the amount. Record the amount within a week of finding it out.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: By 1 March of each year in which a farmer has a derogation, they must have recorded the size of the agricultural area of their holding in hectares (updated within one month if it changes).
source_paragraphs:
By 1 March of each year in which you have a derogation, you must have the following information recorded:
the size of the agricultural area of your holding in hectares (update within one month if this changes)

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: By 1 March of each year in which a farmer has a derogation, they must have recorded the size of the area of grassland for that calendar year in hectares (updated within one month if it changes).
source_paragraphs:
By 1 March of each year in which you have a derogation, you must have the following information recorded:
the size of the area of grassland for that calendar year in hectares (update within one month if this changes)

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: By 1 March of each year in which a farmer has a derogation, they must have recorded a written description of the livestock housing and manure storage systems on their farm, including the volume of manure storage available.
source_paragraphs:
By 1 March of each year in which you have a derogation, you must have the following information recorded:
a written description of the livestock housing and manure storage systems you have on your farm, including the volume of the manure storage available

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: By 1 March of each year in which a farmer has a derogation, they must have recorded the numbers and type of livestock they expect to have on their holding during the remaining part of the calendar year.
source_paragraphs:
By 1 March of each year in which you have a derogation, you must have the following information recorded:
the numbers and type of livestock you expect to have on your holding during the remaining part of the calendar year

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: By 1 March of each year in which a farmer has a derogation, they must have recorded an estimate of the manure nitrogen and phosphate that their livestock will produce during the current calendar year.
source_paragraphs:
By 1 March of each year in which you have a derogation, you must have the following information recorded:
an estimate of the manure nitrogen and phosphate that your livestock will produce during the current calendar year

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder must send the Environment Agency details about their farming practices and fertiliser use for the period 1 January to 31 December by 30 April in the year following the derogation.
source_paragraphs: You must send the EA details about your farming practices and fertiliser use for the period 1 January to 31 December. You must send the details by 30 April in the year following the derogation. This is your fertilisation account.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A derogation holder's fertilisation account must show the total agricultural area of their derogated holding and the area in hectares covered by specified crops including winter wheat, spring wheat, winter barley, spring barley, winter oilseed rape, sugar beet, potatoes, forage maize, and grass.
source_paragraphs:
Your fertilisation account must show the total agricultural area of your derogated holding and the area (in hectares) covered by each of the following crops:
winter wheat
spring wheat
winter barley
spring barley
winter oilseed rape
sugar beet
potatoes
forage maize
grass

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The fertilisation account must show the area covered by other crops (for example, vegetables, lucerne, flowers), but the specific crop does not need to be named.
source_paragraphs: You need to show the area covered by other crops (for example, vegetables, lucerne, flowers), but the specific crop does not need to be named.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The fertilisation plan must show the number and category of livestock kept on the farm and the amount of nitrogen and phosphate in the manure they produce.
source_paragraphs:
Your fertilisation plan must also show the:
number and category of livestock kept on your farm, and the amount of nitrogen and phosphate in the manure they produce (according to the categories in the standard values tables ( 128 KB ) )

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The fertilisation plan must show the amount and type of livestock manure brought on or sent off the farm, together with the total amount of nitrogen and phosphate in that manure.
source_paragraphs: amount and type of livestock manure brought on or sent off your farm, together with the total amount of nitrogen and phosphate in that manure

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The fertilisation plan must show the weight in tonnes and nitrogen content of all manufactured nitrogen fertiliser stocks kept on, brought in, or sent off the farm during the calendar year.
source_paragraphs: weight in tonnes and nitrogen content of all manufactured nitrogen fertiliser stocks kept on, brought in or sent off your farm during the calendar year

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The Environment Agency may inspect a derogation holder's farm to make sure they are meeting the conditions of their derogation.
source_paragraphs: The EA may inspect your farm to make sure you're meeting conditions of your derogation.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A person who uses any manufactured fertilisers, manures or other materials that contain nitrogen on agricultural land in a nitrate vulnerable zone (NVZ) must follow the NVZ nitrogen fertiliser guidance.
source_paragraphs: You must follow this guidance if you use any manufactured fertilisers, manures or other materials that contain nitrogen on agricultural land in a nitrate vulnerable zone ( NVZ ).

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A person who produces or imports livestock manures must also follow the guidance on storing organic manures in NVZs and storing silage, slurry and agricultural fuel oil.
source_paragraphs: You must also follow the guidance on storing organic manures in NVZs and storing silage, slurry and agricultural fuel oil if you produce or import livestock manures.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: There is a limit on the average amount of manufactured fertiliser and crop-available nitrogen from organic manure that can be applied to most crops each year, known as the N-max limit.
source_paragraphs: There's a limit on the average amount of manufactured fertiliser and crop-available nitrogen from organic manure that you can apply to most crops each year - this is known as the N-max limit.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager may apply an additional 80kg of nitrogen per hectare if straw or paper sludge has been used on the previous or current crop.
source_paragraphs: You can use an additional 80kg of nitrogen per hectare if you've used straw or paper sludge on the previous or current crop.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: For wheat and barley, a land manager may use an additional 20kg of nitrogen per hectare for every tonne that the expected yield exceeds the standard yield.
source_paragraphs: For wheat and barley, you can use an additional 20kg of nitrogen per hectare for every tonne that the expected yield exceeds the standard yield.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: On milling wheat varieties, a land manager may use an additional 40kg of nitrogen per hectare.
source_paragraphs: On milling wheat varieties, you can use an additional 40kg of nitrogen per hectare.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: On autumn and winter-sown wheat and winter barley, a land manager may use an additional 20kg of nitrogen per hectare on fields with a shallow soil type, except on shallow soils over sandstone.
source_paragraphs: On autumn and winter-sown wheat and winter barley you can use an additional 20kg of nitrogen per hectare on fields with a shallow soil type (except on shallow soils over sandstone).

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: On winter oilseed rape a land manager may use up to 250kg of nitrogen per hectare, including a maximum autumn (closed period) application of 30kg of nitrogen per hectare of manufactured nitrogen fertiliser.
source_paragraphs: On winter oilseed rape you can use up to 250kg of nitrogen per hectare. This includes a maximum autumn (closed period) application of 30kg of nitrogen per hectare of manufactured nitrogen fertiliser.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: On grass cut at least 3 times in a year, a land manager may use an additional 40kg of nitrogen per hectare.
source_paragraphs: On grass that's cut at least 3 times in a year, you can use an additional 40kg of nitrogen per hectare.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager growing grass to achieve a protein content of at least 16% in the dried product may use nitrogen up to the level recommended in writing by a FACTS-qualified adviser.
source_paragraphs: You can use nitrogen up to the level recommended in writing by a FACTS-qualified adviser if you're growing grass to achieve a protein content of at least 16% in the dried product.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If the land is irrigated, a land manager must not use more than 700kg of nitrogen per hectare.
source_paragraphs: If the land is irrigated, you must not use more than 700kg of nitrogen per hectare.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If the land is not irrigated, a land manager must not use more than 500kg of nitrogen per hectare.
source_paragraphs: If the land isn't irrigated, you must not use more than 500kg of nitrogen per hectare.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: In subsequent years, a land manager must sample irrigated or high-nitrogen fields between 1 September and 31 October for soil mineral nitrogen levels and give the results to their FACTS-qualified adviser.
source_paragraphs: In subsequent years, you must sample these fields between 1 September and 31 October for soil mineral nitrogen levels and give your FACTS-qualified adviser the results.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager may apply up to 170kg per hectare of nitrogen in livestock manure (including manure deposited directly by livestock and spreading) on their holding in each calendar year as a loading limit averaged across the holding.
source_paragraphs: You can apply up to 170kg per hectare of nitrogen in livestock manure (including manure deposited directly by livestock and spreading) on your holding in each calendar year. This limit is the loading limit and applies as an average across your holding. It's separate from the field limit of 250kg per hectare from organic manures.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not use more than 250kg of total nitrogen from all organic manures spread in any 12-month period on any single hectare of land (the field limit), not including livestock manures deposited by grazing animals.
source_paragraphs: You must not use more than 250kg of total nitrogen from all organic manures spread in any 12 month period on any single hectare of your land. This limit (the field limit) doesn't include livestock manures deposited by grazing animals.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must use standard values to work out how much nitrogen is produced by livestock on or brought onto their farm.
source_paragraphs: You must use standard values to work out how much nitrogen is produced by the livestock on your farm or bought on to your farm.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must plan their nitrogen use so that they do not exceed the livestock manure nitrogen loading limit.
source_paragraphs: You must plan so that you don't exceed the limit.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If the only organic manure used is certified green or certified green/food compost, a land manager may apply up to 500kg of nitrogen per hectare every 2 years as mulch or worked into the ground.
source_paragraphs: up to 500kg of nitrogen per hectare every 2 years as mulch or worked into the ground

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If the only organic manure used is certified green or certified green/food compost, a land manager may apply up to 1,000kg of nitrogen per hectare every 4 years only as mulch and only in an orchard growing fruit of the genera Malus, Prunus or Pyrus.
source_paragraphs: up to 1,000kg of nitrogen per hectare every 4 years (only as mulch and in an orchard growing fruit of the genera Malus, Prunus or Pyrus)

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The compost used under the certified green/green-food compost exemption must not contain livestock manure and must be produced to the PAS100 protocol.
source_paragraphs: The compost that you use must not contain livestock manure and must be produced to the PAS100 protocol.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must plan all applications of nitrogen on each crop in each field (including grass), and must keep the fertilisation plan as part of farm records.
source_paragraphs: You must plan all your applications of nitrogen on each crop in each field (including grass). This is your fertilisation plan. You must keep it as part of your farm records.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before applying nitrogen for the first time in a field where a crop is to be or has been planted, a land manager must calculate the amount of nitrogen in the soil likely to be available for the crop during the growing season.
source_paragraphs: Calculate the amount of nitrogen in the soil that's likely to be available for the crop to use during the growing season.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before applying nitrogen for the first time in a field where a crop is to be or has been planted, a land manager must calculate the optimum amount of nitrogen that should be applied to the crop, taking into account the amount of nitrogen already available in the soil.
source_paragraphs: Calculate the optimum amount of nitrogen that should be applied to the crop, taking into account the amount of nitrogen already available in the soil.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before applying nitrogen for the first time in a field, a land manager must calculate the amount of nitrogen from any planned applications of organic manure that is likely to be available to the crop in the growing season in which it is spread.
source_paragraphs: Calculate the amount of nitrogen from any planned applications of organic manure that's likely to be available to the crop in the growing season in which you spread it.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before applying nitrogen for the first time in a field, a land manager must calculate the amount of manufactured nitrogen fertiliser needed.
source_paragraphs: Calculate the amount of manufactured nitrogen fertiliser you need.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: In subsequent growing seasons, before applying nitrogen to any crop or land where a crop is to be planted (including grass), a land manager must repeat the soil nitrogen supply and optimum nitrogen application calculations and prepare a plan for fertiliser use for that growing season.
source_paragraphs:
In subsequent growing seasons, before you apply nitrogen to any crop or land where you're going to plant a crop (including grass) you must:
repeat steps 1 and 2
prepare a plan for your fertiliser use for that growing season

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before applying livestock manure, a land manager must calculate the total amount of nitrogen in the manure, using standard values or results from sampling and analysis.
source_paragraphs:
Before you apply livestock manure, you must calculate the:
total amount of nitrogen in the manure, using standard values or results from sampling and analysis
amount of crop-available nitrogen in the manure

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Before applying livestock manure, a land manager must calculate the amount of crop-available nitrogen in the manure.
source_paragraphs:
Before you apply livestock manure, you must calculate the:
total amount of nitrogen in the manure, using standard values or results from sampling and analysis
amount of crop-available nitrogen in the manure

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread any organic manure on crops with an N-max limit unless they have used an approved method to work out the crop-available nitrogen in the manure before applying it.
source_paragraphs: You must not spread any organic manure unless you have used one of these methods to work out the crop-available nitrogen in the manure before applying it to crops that have an N-max limit.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: It is an offence to allow fertiliser or organic manure to enter surface water such as rivers or ponds.
source_paragraphs: It's an offence to allow fertiliser or organic manure to enter surface water (such as rivers or ponds).

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must inspect the field to assess the risk of nitrogen getting into surface water before spreading any fertilisers or organic manures.
source_paragraphs: You must inspect the field to assess the risk of nitrogen getting into surface water (for example, through runoff) before you spread any fertilisers or organic manures.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread any manufactured fertilisers or organic manures on a field that is waterlogged, flooded or covered in snow.
source_paragraphs:
You must not spread any manufactured fertilisers or organic manures if a field is either:
waterlogged, flooded or covered in snow
frozen for more than 12 hours in the previous 24 hours

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread any manufactured fertilisers or organic manures on a field that has been frozen for more than 12 hours in the previous 24 hours.
source_paragraphs:
You must not spread any manufactured fertilisers or organic manures if a field is either:
waterlogged, flooded or covered in snow
frozen for more than 12 hours in the previous 24 hours

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread manufactured nitrogen fertiliser within 2 metres of surface water.
source_paragraphs:
You must not spread:
manufactured nitrogen fertiliser within 2 metres of surface water
organic manure within 50 metres of a spring, well or borehole or 10 metres of surface water

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread organic manure within 50 metres of a spring, well or borehole.
source_paragraphs:
You must not spread:
manufactured nitrogen fertiliser within 2 metres of surface water
organic manure within 50 metres of a spring, well or borehole or 10 metres of surface water

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread organic manure within 10 metres of surface water.
source_paragraphs:
You must not spread:
manufactured nitrogen fertiliser within 2 metres of surface water
organic manure within 50 metres of a spring, well or borehole or 10 metres of surface water

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must only spread manufactured nitrogen fertilisers and manures on agricultural land that is being used to grow crops (including grass).
source_paragraphs: You must only spread manufactured nitrogen fertilisers and manures on agricultural land that you're using to grow crops (including grass).

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must spread manufactured nitrogen fertilisers and organic manures as accurately as possible.
source_paragraphs: You must spread manufactured nitrogen fertilisers and organic manures as accurately as possible.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager may spread slurry, sewage sludge and anaerobic digestate no less than 6 metres from surface water if precision manure spreading equipment such as band spreaders, shallow injectors or dribble-bar applicators is used.
source_paragraphs:
You can spread slurry, sewage sludge and anaerobic digestate no less than 6 metres from surface water if you use precision manure spreading equipment like:
band spreaders (trailing hose or trailing shoe)
shallow injectors (that inject no more than 10cm below the surface)
dribble-bar applicators

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Straw-based solid manure spread within 10 metres of surface water on land notified as a site of special scientific interest or managed under an agri-environment scheme must only be spread between 1 June and 31 October, must not be spread directly into surface water, and must not exceed 12.5 tonnes per hectare each year.
source_paragraphs:
You must only spread between 1 June and 31 October and not:
directly into surface water
more than 12.5 tonnes per hectare each year

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: High readily available nitrogen manures are organic fertilisers that have more than 30% of their total nitrogen content immediately available to crops.
source_paragraphs: Some organic fertilisers have more than 30% of their total nitrogen content immediately available to crops. These are called 'high readily available nitrogen manures'.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread high readily available nitrogen manures on or between the dates shown in the closed period table.
source_paragraphs: You must not spread high readily available nitrogen manures on or between the dates shown in this table.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Soil is classified as shallow if it is less than 40cm deep.
source_paragraphs: Your soil is shallow if it's less than 40cm deep

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread more than 150kg of total nitrogen per hectare of high readily available nitrogen manure in a single application.
source_paragraphs: You must not spread more than 150kg of total nitrogen per hectare.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: From the end of the closed period until the end of February, a land manager must not spread more than 30m³/ha of slurry in a single application.
source_paragraphs:
You must not spread more than 150kg of total nitrogen per hectare.
You must not spread more than 30 m 3 /ha of slurry or 8 tonnes/ha of poultry manure in a single application from the end of the closed period until the end of February.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: From the end of the closed period until the end of February, a land manager must not spread more than 8 tonnes/ha of poultry manure in a single application.
source_paragraphs: You must not spread more than 30 m 3 /ha of slurry or 8 tonnes/ha of poultry manure in a single application from the end of the closed period until the end of February.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must allow at least 3 weeks between each individual application of high readily available nitrogen manure from the end of the closed period until the end of February.
source_paragraphs: You must allow at least 3 weeks between each individual application.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must only spread slurry using precision spreading equipment or equipment that has a low spreading trajectory (below 4 metres from the ground) or spreads slurry at a maximum rate of no more than 1 millimetre per hour when operating continuously.
source_paragraphs:
You must only spread slurry using precision spreading equipment or equipment that either:
has a low spreading trajectory (below 4 metres from the ground)
spreads slurry at a maximum rate of no more than 1 millimetre per hour when operating continuously

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When spreading manure on bare soil or stubble not sown with seed, a land manager must work poultry manure, slurry and liquid-digested sludge into the soil as soon as practically possible and within 24 hours at the latest.
source_paragraphs:
When you spread manure on bare soil or stubble (except if it's been sown with seed), you must:
work poultry manure, slurry and liquid-digested sludge into the soil (for example, by ploughing) as soon as it's practically possible to do so and within 24 hours at the latest

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When spreading manure on bare soil or stubble not sown with seed on sloping land within 50 metres of surface water that could receive run-off, a land manager must work any organic manure (unless spread as mulch on sandy soil) into the soil as soon as possible and within 24 hours at the latest.
source_paragraphs: work any organic manure into the soil (unless it's been spread as mulch on sandy soil) as soon as possible and within 24 hours at the latest if the land is sloping and within 50 metres of surface water that could receive run-off from it

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager does not have to work in slurry and liquid-digested sludge if it has been applied using a trailing hose, shoe band spreader, dribble bar applicator or an injector.
source_paragraphs: You don't have to work in slurry and liquid-digested sludge if you have applied it using a trailing hose, shoe band spreader, dribble bar applicator or an injector.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread manufactured nitrogen fertiliser on grassland during the closed period from 15 September to 15 January.
source_paragraphs:
You must not spread manufactured nitrogen fertiliser on or between the following dates (closed periods):
from 15 September to 15 January on grassland
from 1 September to 15 January on tillage land

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must not spread manufactured nitrogen fertiliser on tillage land during the closed period from 1 September to 15 January.
source_paragraphs:
You must not spread manufactured nitrogen fertiliser on or between the following dates (closed periods):
from 15 September to 15 January on grassland
from 1 September to 15 January on tillage land

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a land manager grows crops not listed in the closed-period exemptions table, they must have written advice from a FACTS-qualified adviser before spreading manufactured nitrogen fertilisers during the closed period.
source_paragraphs: If you grow crops that aren't listed in the table, you must have written advice from a FACTS-qualified adviser before you spread manufactured nitrogen fertilisers.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Limits on fertiliser use do not apply to land inside greenhouses, glasshouses and polytunnels where the land is enclosed for the whole calendar year.
source_paragraphs: You don't need to keep to limits on fertiliser use on land inside greenhouses, glasshouses and polytunnels where the land is enclosed for the whole calendar year. If land is exposed to the open air at any time (for example, if you uncover a polytunnel) the limits apply for the whole of that year.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If land inside a greenhouse, glasshouse or polytunnel is exposed to the open air at any time during the year, the nitrogen fertiliser limits apply for the whole of that year.
source_paragraphs: If land is exposed to the open air at any time (for example, if you uncover a polytunnel) the limits apply for the whole of that year.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager does not need to keep records of nitrogen fertiliser use or the yield of arable crops on land inside a greenhouse.
source_paragraphs: You don't need to keep records of your use of nitrogen fertilisers or the yield of arable crops in a greenhouse.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A low-intensity farmer is one where at least 80% of their land is grassland, no more than 100kg of nitrogen per hectare per year is applied as organic manure, no more than 90kg of nitrogen per hectare per year is spread as manufactured fertiliser, and no organic manure is brought onto the holding.
source_paragraphs:
You're a low-intensity farmer if all of the following apply to you:
at least 80% of your land is grassland
you apply no more than 100kg of nitrogen per hectare per year as organic manure (including any nitrogen in manure deposited on the field by livestock)
you spread no more than 90kg of nitrogen per hectare per year as manufactured fertiliser
you don't bring any organic manure onto your holding

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A low-intensity farmer does not have to keep a record of their actual applications of manufactured fertiliser and organic manure in each field.
source_paragraphs: You don't have to keep a record of your actual applications of manufactured fertiliser and organic manure in each field.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A low-intensity farmer must have recorded information to show that they meet the criteria for low-intensity farms.
source_paragraphs: You must have recorded information to show that you meet the criteria for low-intensity farms.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A low-intensity farmer must still plan their nitrogen use by keeping a fertilisation plan.
source_paragraphs: You must still plan your nitrogen use by keeping a fertilisation plan.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: When calculating fertiliser applications, a land manager must not include any area of their holding where no fertiliser is spread or the soil is not worked, such as rough grazing areas.
source_paragraphs: When calculating your fertiliser applications, you must not include any area of your holding where you don't spread any fertiliser or work the soil (for example, on rough grazing areas).

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must keep all records of their fertiliser use for at least 5 years.
source_paragraphs: You must keep all records of your fertiliser use for at least 5 years.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must keep records of each step in their fertilisation plan for each field in which nitrogen fertiliser is used.
source_paragraphs: You must keep records of each step in your fertilisation plan for each field in which you use nitrogen fertiliser.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must keep a copy of any advice from a FACTS-qualified adviser with their fertilisation plan.
source_paragraphs: You must also keep a copy of any advice from a FACTS-qualified adviser with your plan.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must update their field records within 1 week of sowing, spreading fertiliser or harvesting a crop.
source_paragraphs: You must update your field records within 1 week of sowing, spreading fertiliser or harvesting a crop.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must keep evidence of the soil nitrogen supply and how it was calculated.
source_paragraphs:
You must keep evidence of:
the soil nitrogen supply and how you calculated it
the crop nitrogen requirement and how you calculated it
any written advice from a FACTS-qualified adviser

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must keep evidence of the crop nitrogen requirement and how it was calculated.
source_paragraphs:
You must keep evidence of:
the soil nitrogen supply and how you calculated it
the crop nitrogen requirement and how you calculated it
any written advice from a FACTS-qualified adviser

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must keep evidence of any written advice from a FACTS-qualified adviser.
source_paragraphs:
You must keep evidence of:
the soil nitrogen supply and how you calculated it
the crop nitrogen requirement and how you calculated it
any written advice from a FACTS-qualified adviser

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must keep original laboratory reports of any sampling and analysis done to find out the nitrogen content in organic manure used.
source_paragraphs: You must keep original laboratory reports of any sampling and analysis you have done to find out the nitrogen content in organic manure that you use.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must record the yield of any arable crop on which nitrogen fertiliser has been used within one week of finding it out.
source_paragraphs: You must record the yield of any arable crop on which nitrogen fertiliser has been used, within one week of finding it out.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must keep an up-to-date record of the total size of their holding and update it within 1 month if it changes (except where the change in area is land covered by a greenhouse).
source_paragraphs: You must keep an up-to-date record of the total size of your holding and update it within 1 month if it changes. This applies to you if the change in area isn't land covered by a greenhouse.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The total size of a holding must include any area not covered by greenhouses and excludes surface waters, any hardstanding, buildings, roads or any woodland unless that woodland is used for grazing.
source_paragraphs: The total size of your holding must include any area not covered by greenhouses and excludes surface waters, any hardstanding (areas for parking vehicles), buildings, roads or any woodland (unless that woodland is used for grazing).

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager who spreads organic manure must make a risk map and keep it with their farm records.
source_paragraphs: You must make a risk map and keep it with your farm records if you spread organic manure on your land.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must mark on the risk map the location of each field and its area in hectares.
source_paragraphs:
You must mark on the map:
the location of each field and its area in hectares
areas with sandy or shallow soils
land with a slope greater than 12 degrees
land drains (except if they are sealed and impermeable)
sites where you plan to use temporary field heaps to store manure
all surface waters (for example, streams or ponds) and land within 10 metres of them
all springs, wells and boreholes on your land or within 50 metres of the boundary of your land
all land within 50 metres of a spring, well or borehole
low run-off risk land (if you intend to spread to this land to reduce the amount of storage you need to provide)

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must mark on the risk map all surface waters (for example, streams or ponds) and land within 10 metres of them.
source_paragraphs: all surface waters (for example, streams or ponds) and land within 10 metres of them

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must mark on the risk map all springs, wells and boreholes on their land or within 50 metres of the boundary of their land.
source_paragraphs: all springs, wells and boreholes on your land or within 50 metres of the boundary of your land

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager must update the risk map with any changes within 3 months of the date of the change.
source_paragraphs: You must update the map with any changes within 3 months of the date of the change.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: For the previous calendar year, a land manager must complete a record by 30 April showing the area of the holding in hectares, the numbers of livestock kept, the type and number of days each animal spent on the holding, and their calculation of the amount of nitrogen produced by livestock.
source_paragraphs:
For the previous calendar year, you must complete a record by 30 April showing:
the area of your holding in hectares
the numbers of livestock kept on your holding
the type of animal ('category' in the standard tables) and number of days each animal spent on your holding
your calculation of the amount of nitrogen produced by livestock

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Within 1 week of bringing livestock manure onto or sending it off their holding, a land manager must record the type and amount of manure and the date it was brought onto or sent off their holding.
source_paragraphs:
Within 1 week of bringing livestock manure (including poultry manure and slurry) onto your holding or sending it off, you must record:
the type and amount of manure and the date it was brought onto or sent off your holding
the total nitrogen content of any manure you send off or bring onto your holding
the name and address of the supplier or recipient of the manure
a contingency plan you'll follow if the manure isn't accepted by a recipient (for example, how you plan to store the manure)

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Within 1 week of bringing livestock manure onto or sending it off their holding, a land manager must record the total nitrogen content of any manure sent off or brought onto their holding.
source_paragraphs:
Within 1 week of bringing livestock manure (including poultry manure and slurry) onto your holding or sending it off, you must record:
the type and amount of manure and the date it was brought onto or sent off your holding
the total nitrogen content of any manure you send off or bring onto your holding
the name and address of the supplier or recipient of the manure
a contingency plan you'll follow if the manure isn't accepted by a recipient (for example, how you plan to store the manure)

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Within 1 week of bringing livestock manure onto or sending it off their holding, a land manager must record the name and address of the supplier or recipient of the manure.
source_paragraphs:
Within 1 week of bringing livestock manure (including poultry manure and slurry) onto your holding or sending it off, you must record:
the type and amount of manure and the date it was brought onto or sent off your holding
the total nitrogen content of any manure you send off or bring onto your holding
the name and address of the supplier or recipient of the manure
a contingency plan you'll follow if the manure isn't accepted by a recipient (for example, how you plan to store the manure)

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: Within 1 week of bringing livestock manure onto or sending it off their holding, a land manager must record a contingency plan to follow if the manure is not accepted by a recipient.
source_paragraphs: a contingency plan you'll follow if the manure isn't accepted by a recipient (for example, how you plan to store the manure)

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: If a land manager does not know the nitrogen content of imported manure, they must find this out by analysis or calculation as soon as possible and then record it within a week.
source_paragraphs: If you don't know the nitrogen content of imported manure, you must find this out (by analysis or calculation) as soon as possible, and then record it within a week.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager who claims direct payments, such as agri-environment payments, must follow the Code of Good Agricultural Practice for nitrates.
source_paragraphs: You must follow the Code of Good Agricultural Practice for nitrates if you claim direct payments, for example, agri-environment payments.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: The Environment Agency enforces the NVZ rules.
source_paragraphs: The Environment Agency enforces the NVZ rules.

guidance_propositions.proposition_text: A land manager who has land in an NVZ and does not comply with the NVZ rules may be prosecuted and fined.
source_paragraphs: If you have land in an NVZ and don't comply with the NVZ rules, you may be prosecuted and fined.

proposition_matches.explanation: The surrounding guidance extensively covers the specific procedural notification requirement (14 days' notice before construction) and the broader storage rules, meaning the guidance as a whole is not incomplete with respect to the law proposition's notice obligation.

This provision is a purely procedural pre-construction notice requirement; the guidance addresses the substantive duty to follow storage rules, not the procedure of notifying the Agency at least 14 days before starting construction. Rule 5 applies — the guidance is about a substantive obligation, not this procedural step.

Regulation 7(1) empowers the Agency to serve notice on whoever has 'custody or control' or is 'responsible for' silage, slurry or fuel oil storage, which provides the nearest legal basis for attributing responsibility. The guidance goes further by specifically describing a tenant's ability to prove a leaseholder is jointly or wholly responsible — a nuance not expressly stated in reg 7(1), making the guidance broader than what this clause alone establishes.

This clause prohibits spreading organic manure within 50 metres of a borehole, spring or well — a substantive operational rule. The guidance concerns penalty/prosecution powers, a different subject matter entirely.

Under Rule 5, this law clause is purely procedural (pre-construction notice to the Agency). The guidance addresses a substantive obligation to follow substance-specific rules for new or substantially changed stores, which is a different point entirely and cannot be anchored on a procedural notice requirement.

This clause requires slurry storage tanks, effluent tanks, channels, pipes and reception pits to last at least 20 years with proper maintenance, which aligns with the guidance's first claim that a new or substantially changed store must have an expected lifespan of at least 20 years with maintenance. The match is medium confidence because the guidance says 'store' generically while the law clause is specific to slurry/effluent infrastructure.

The law requires that no part of the fuel storage area or its bund may be within 10 metres of inland freshwaters or coastal waters that fuel oil could enter if it escaped. The guidance states the store must be at least 10 metres clear, which broadly matches but omits the bund element and the qualifying condition ('that fuel oil could enter if it were to escape'), making it incomplete.

Rule 1 applies: regulatory_kind is factual_statement, so no law clause can ground this guidance, even though the clause substantively matches the contract-before-March-1991/completed-before-September-1991 condition described.

The exemption in Regulation 6(1)(c)(ii) is conditional on construction/substantial enlargement/reconstruction having been commenced before 1 March 1991 and completed before 1 September 1991. The guidance accurately conveys that undertaking substantial changes (structural changes, increasing capacity, relocating) to a pre-1991 installation removes the exemption, which is the direct legal consequence when those conditions cease to apply.

Regulation 7(2) describes the standard the Agency must apply when specifying required works — reducing to a minimum any significant risk of pollution — which supports the guidance's framing that notices are issued where there is a significant risk of pollution. However, it is a supplementary provision to reg 7(1) rather than the primary anchor.

This regulation sets a specific 50-metre minimum siting distance from watercourses as a floor. The guidance's general statement not to pollute rivers or watercourses when constructing storage is broader than (but consistent with) this specific rule, raising the obligation to a general no-pollution standard rather than a precise distance.

This provision places a duty on the person with custody or control of field silage to ensure the Agency receives at least 14 days' notice before first use of a new site — matching the guidance precisely in both the duty-holder (farmer/person in control), the trigger (new site/first use), and the notice period (14 days).
Rule 1 applies: the guidance is classified as a factual_statement, and factual or background guidance cannot be anchored on a law clause regardless of how closely the law matches the content.

This provision directly prohibits opening or removing the wrapping of a silage bale within 10 metres of inland freshwaters or coastal waters, which precisely matches the guidance's unwrapping element. The guidance accurately reflects this part of the law.

The neighbouring proposition 'A farmer must not make or store any silage, or unwrap baled silage, within 10 metres of inland or coastal waters' directly covers the missing 10-metre requirement for inland/coastal waters identified in the verdict, resolving the specific incompleteness concern.

This clause concerns risk mapping obligations for organic manure spreading — an entirely different substantive area from the definition of a protected water supply source. No definitional or conceptual overlap justifies anchoring the guidance here.

The law applies only 'so far as reasonably practicable' and specifies particular components (base, walls, effluent tank, channels, pipe walls), whereas the guidance states that 'all parts' must be resistant without qualification — this exceeds both the scope and the qualified standard set by the law.

This clause requires the base to extend beyond any walls, which the guidance reflects accurately. However, the guidance adds the impermeability requirement not present in this clause, making the guidance broader than this provision alone.

This provision requires drainage from perimeter channels to an effluent tank via a channel or pipe, which matches the guidance's statement that drainage channels must flow into an effluent tank. The guidance accurately reflects this legal requirement.

The law requires the silo base to comply with BS 8007:1987 only; the guidance adds a further requirement for compliance with BS 8110-1:1997, raising a higher bar than the statutory minimum without contradicting it.

Both the guidance and this law clause sit within the same regulatory framework and address the same point — the hot-rolled asphalt standard for silo bases — but they specify different standards (BS 594/EN 13108-4:2006 in the guidance vs. BS 5502:Part 21:1990 in the law), which is a direct substantive conflict on the same requirement.

The guidance states that silo walls must withstand wall loadings set in BS 5502-22:2003+A1:2013, which accurately reflects the law's requirement that retaining walls must withstand minimum wall loadings calculated per paragraph 15.6 of BS 5502: Part 22:2003. The reference to the +A1:2013 amendment is a minor addition that does not contradict the law.

The neighbouring proposition 'A silo must have impermeable drainage collection channels around the outside, flowing into an effluent tank' specifically covers the perimeter channel requirement that the reason identified as missing, resolving the incompleteness concern.

This clause requires slurry storage tanks and effluent tanks to last at least 20 years with proper maintenance, which aligns with the guidance's 20-year with-maintenance standard for above-ground effluent tanks. The guidance accurately reflects this requirement, though it adds the specific condition 'all parts above ground' as the scenario context.

The neighbouring proposition that underground effluent tank parts must 'last 20 years without maintenance' covers the structural integrity requirement, resolving the specific concern that only impermeability was mentioned.

This provision concerns the capacity of slurry stores to accommodate rainfall and other liquids, not a prohibition on introducing silage effluent into under-floor slurry stores. It is from a different subject-matter and does not support the guidance.

This candidate states exactly that silage bales must be wrapped and sealed in impermeable membranes or enclosed in impermeable bags, which matches the guidance precisely. The guidance accurately reflects this provision.

The surrounding guidance explicitly states 'A farmer must keep baled silage at least 10 metres clear of inland or coastal waters,' directly covering the specific 10-metre distance requirement identified as missing in the original verdict.

The guidance accurately reflects the 10-metre requirement for storing baled silage near inland or coastal waters, but omits the important qualifier that the rule applies to waters 'which effluent escaping from the bales could enter' — a condition that narrows the scope of the obligation. The guidance also omits any mention of protected water supply source abstraction point requirements if such exist for bales.
This provision concerns distance requirements from water bodies and abstraction points, not the absence of construction works or topsoil disturbance. Cross-topic mismatch within silage regulations.
